exhibit.surface: UI browse page (not the GraphQL probe)

got.title: COSHH Online Course With Instant Certificate or Get Lifetime Access to 2500+ Online Courses
got.note: Workplace safety training, delivered online. Not a skydive at any distance.

got.title: Skydive South West — Experience the Thrill of Skydiving, Solo or Duo, 7,000ft to 15,000ft
got.note: A real skydive — in Dunkeswell, Devon, 141.5 miles from London.

exhibit.mechanism: The matcher matches fragments of the query, not the query. On the same host, `kitesurf` returns a "Portable Bartender Barista Kit" — matched on `kit`.
exhibit.hinge: A dashboard records this as two results returned. Neither answers the question, and for a customer in London there is nothing here at all. So how many results came back cannot tell you whether search worked — which is why the rest of this page asks a different question.
exhibit.counterpoint: Groupon **can** say it has nothing: `kitesurf` on the same London-filtered page returns 0 deals and a proper empty state. The failure is not that it never admits defeat — it is that it does not admit defeat when fragment matching produces one or two irrelevant results. That is the 1–2 band in chapter 1.

got: London Cable Car + Uber Boat Hop-On Hop-Off 1 Day River Pass
London: London Cable Car + Uber Boat One Way River Thames Cruise
Automatic Flying Magic Wings for Kids
Vivo Folding Clothes Drying Rack with Height Adjustable Side Wing
One, Two or Three Senecio Angel Wings Potted Plants
VIP Desert Safari with BBQ Dinner & 30-Min Quad Bike
substitution.why: Third result is a children's toy — a Good, not an experience.

no_lever.set_test: massage vs paintball massage at limit 100: 92 of 99 ids shared, Jaccard 0.868. The paintball deals are blended INTO a massage result set.
no_lever.claim: The result count is not a function of specificity, and does not track whether the catalogue stocks the thing. The user has no lever.
no_lever.not_claimed: NOT union semantics — helicopter contradicts it, as do the dinosaur pairs and shark diving from 2026-08-05.

returns: cards[] — id, title, url, merchant, prices, rating, badges, discountPercentage
facets[] — distance, locations, price, categories, bookable, sort
pagination — limit, offset, nextOffset, feedToken, totalCount
absent: any spell-correction or 'did you mean' field
response.consequence: The client receives a count and a list and cannot tell a genuine match from padding. That is exactly the supplied dataset's limitation — results_shown is a bare count with no query→deal mapping. The dataset does not understate production; it reproduces it.

distance.claim: The platform computes a distance histogram on every call. For thin queries it is empty at every radius — 2 results that sit nowhere near the user, returned anyway.

supply.note: Single-token queries only. Multi-word counts (hot air balloon = 558) are inflated by the fragment matching above and are NOT a measure of supply — reading them as one is the mistake this table exists to correct.
supply.bound: So the supplied catalogue's TOTAL void — 0 deals, 100% zero rate — exaggerates a real thinness rather than inventing one. The shape the analysis identifies is visible in production at less extreme magnitude. That means this package may claim the pattern is not merely an artifact of synthetic data. It may NOT put a number on real Groupon's inventory gap, or recommend vendor acquisition in a named city.
supply.correction: This table replaced an earlier one that claimed London stocks adrenaline 'abundantly', on the strength of multi-word counts. That evidence was an artifact of the very defect described above. Probing Berlin and Paris with single tokens exposed it the same day.

exactly_three.claim: Live returns exactly 3 routinely. The supplied data has 0, 1, 2 then jumps to 4 across 8,997 searches — so that gap is a generator artifact, not a ranking cutoff.

autocomplete.detail: 3 of 4 queries on groupon.pl, 2026-08-06; 5 of 5 on groupon.co.uk, 2026-08-05. Cross-host and cross-day, so not a session artifact.
autocomplete.claim: The layer where spell correction and query understanding live is returning nothing.

rows.label: Nowhere in the market
rows.what: Nothing in this market's catalogue answers it — in any city, all month.
rows.reading: Search cannot fix this at any quality. That is the finding, not a limitation of it: you cannot sell a skydive you do not have.

rows.label: The user's own city
rows.what: A deal answering the query was stocked in that city, that month. The search still failed.
rows.reading: This is the search problem, and this is its actual size.

rows.label: Another city in the market
rows.what: Stocked in the market, never where the searcher was.
rows.reading: Small, and it stays small for a reason — this bucket is haircuts, nails and gym passes, not skydives. Nobody travels to the next city for a haircut, so widening the radius would not rescue it.

rows.label: Can't tell from this catalogue
rows.what: A generic deal might or might not answer it, or the query could not be mapped to a concept at all.
rows.reading: One dead end in five we cannot honestly place. A generic "Three-Course Meal for Two" is not an answer to `burger` — but it is not proof there wasn't one either.

sensitivity.seam: `plausible` coverage — a generic deal that might or might not answer the query. All 1,016 of these dead ends move together.

classes.what: Nothing in the catalogue answers it, ever.

classes.label: Baseline residual
classes.what: Stocked, still dead ~40% of the time. Unexplained.

controls.name: It is not simply “English words”
controls.detail: Loanwords used in every market — brunch, crossfit, sushi, paintball, bowling — are also English-origin. They dead-end at 44.0% (497/1129), the ordinary rate, not 81%. They name concepts the catalogue does not stock: their problem is supply.

controls.name: It is not “rare queries just fail more”
controls.detail: The English arm is low-volume (240 searches vs 2,345). But rare local-language queries (n≤5) dead-end at 53.3%, not 81%, and there is no rarity gradient among local queries at all.

language.caveat: This is synthetic data. What it demonstrates is that the generator encoded a language effect — evidence the brief's own thesis is coherent and quantifiable, not independent proof that Groupon production search has this exact defect.

assumptions.label: Supply void
assumptions.basis: ZERO BY CONSTRUCTION. No inventory exists. Search cannot fix this at any quality — that is the finding, not a limitation of the estimate.

assumptions.label: Silent substitution
assumptions.basis: DELIBERATE ZERO. The fix makes a false-confident page honest; it may reduce near-term clicks. The return is trust, which this data cannot measure.

assumptions.label: Unexplained residual
assumptions.basis: WITHDRAWN 2026-08-06. Was 40%, resting entirely on 'no search returns exactly 3, so there must be a cutoff'. Live Groupon returns 3 routinely, so the inference is dead and this is a second unexplained residual.

assumptions.label: Uneven across cities
assumptions.basis: ASSUMPTION, AND ITS STATED BASIS IS NOW KNOWN TO BE WRONG. The 25% was justified as 'inventory exists in-market, not in-city, so offer a wider radius'. Chapter 3 tested that: only 6 of this class's 321 dead ends have the deal in another city. The RANGE IS DELIBERATELY LEFT UNCHANGED rather than re-derived, because re-deriving it lowers the headline and we would rather report the number that is generous to search. Tightening it is shown below.

assumptions.label: Language / phrasing
assumptions.basis: MEASURED. English phrasing dead-ends 81.2% vs 39.0% local — a 42.3pp gap on 81.2% of volume means 52% of this class is language, not supply.
